abstract: Abstract Transcriptional quality control is essential to maintain the integrity of genetic information. Although well characterized in yeast and metazoans, the regulation of transcriptional fidelity in plants remains elusive. We explored transcriptional fidelity and alternative splicing control in Arabidopsis thaliana using genetic, molecular biology, and deep sequencing tools. Using circle-sequencing assays, we analyzed the error landscape of the transcriptome at single-nucleotide depth under ambient and heat-stress conditions in wild-type and different quality control mutant plants. We found that the frequency of nucleotide misincorporations and insertions is significantly elevated under heat stress, and that nucleotide imbalance also leads to error-prone transcription. We demonstrate that the RNA polymerase II-associated elongation cofactor TFIIS is a fidelity factor for both transcription and alternative splicing, as its absence reduces the accuracy of both processes. Moreover, we found that the nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) cytoplasmic surveillance system is also required for heat-stress tolerance: NMD degrades transcripts containing premature termination codons, generated by 1 to 2 nucleotide indels of erroneous transcription and by alternative splicing during heat stress. In conclusion, the interplay between these RNA surveillance systems safeguards the correct genetic information flow and is critical for developmental regulation and heat-stress adaptation in plants.
methods:
Materials and methods
Plant materials
Arabidopsis seeds were bleach sterilized, stratified for 2 days in the dark and plated on Murashige and Skoog (Duchefa M0222,
https://duchefa-biochemie.com
) medium agar plates (0.5× Murashige and Skoog salts, 0.5% sucrose, 1% agar, pH 5.8). Plants were routinely grown in a Sanyo MLR-350 growth cabinet under cool white light at 21 °C long-day condition (16 h light/8 h dark).
The
tfIIs-1;upf3-1
plants are sterile at 21° C but can produce very low amounts of viable seed at 25 °C; this gives us the opportunity to obtain seeds. Further molecular works using these seeds were performed under standard conditions (on seedlings grown at 21 °C).
Mutant and transgenic lines used in the study
tfIIs-1
(SALK_056755) (
Grasser et al. 2009
),
upf1-5
(SALK_081178) (
Arciga-Reyes et al. 2006
),
upf3-1
(SALK_025175) (
Arciga-Reyes et al. 2006
). Mutant seeds were ordered from NASC (
https://arabidopsis.info
).
upf3-1
seeds were donated by K. Riha lab. By crossing these single mutants, we generated the double mutants used in the study.
Phenotyping analysis
For developmental characterization, Col-0 wild-type,
tfIIs-1, upf1-5, upf3-1, tfIIs;upf1,
and
tfIIs;upf3
plants were grown in a Sanyo MLR-350 growth cabinet under cool white light at 21 °C long-day condition (16 h light/8 h dark) in soil. Three-week-old plants were examined using an automatized PlantScreen Modular high-throughput phenotyping system (Photon System Instruments Ltd, PSI, Brno). The measurements consisted of a 20-min dark adaptation period at 21 °C inside the acclimation chamber followed by chlorophyll fluorescence, RGB, and hyperspectral imaging. The morphological (plant area, diameter, eccentricity) and physiological (TCARI,
F
v
/
F
m
) parameters were determined from the image analysis with the use of PlantScreen software tool package according to the software instructions (PSI, Brno). Color segmentation analysis was performed also from the RGB images: the size of the circles represents the number of pixels in each color class (
n
= 10). Statistical analysis is shown in
Supplementary Table S4
.
Heat stress treatments
For HS treatment regime, TMHT, 7-day-old seedlings were placed in a growing cabinet preheated to 37 °C and kept for 1 to 5 days. During the treatment, long-day conditions were used (16 h light/8 h dark). Treatments were started at midday (Zeitgeber time, ZT8). For molecular works, samples were collected immediately after treatment lasting for 1 hour (1 h), 1 day (1 d), or following a 2-day recovery period (RE). For phenotyping, plants (on agar plates) were treated as described above, then kept at 21 °C for 1 or 2 wk for post-growth, and then photographed. Statistical analysis is shown in
Supplementary Table S4
.
Mycophenolic acid treatment
For MPA treatments, seedlings were pre-grown for 7 days on 0.5× MS containing 0.5% sucrose and 1% agar media plates; on 7th day the seedlings were treated with 0.4 mg/mL MPA (ethanol stock solution 10 mg/mL), or solvent (CTL, ethanol), 2 mL/plate, respectively. For CirSeq library preparation, CTL- or MPA-treated seedlings were collected the next day (24 h treatment); for phenotyping experiments, the CTL- or MPA-treated seedlings were placed in plant growing cabinets and were grown at standard conditions for 14 days. Statistical analysis is shown in
Supplementary Table S4
.
CirSeq library preparations
All materials and reaction conditions for circle-sequencing were done as described previously (
Fritsch et al. 2018
). In brief, after total RNA extraction and polyadenylated RNA purification (to enrich for RNAPII products), the mRNA was enzymatically fragmented and then circularized. The circular RNAs were reverse transcribed during a rolling cycle reaction with a strand-displacing reverse transcriptase (Invitrogen SuperScript III RT; the product contains multiple concatenated units within a long single-molecule cDNA). After this, the single-stranded cDNA was converted into double-stranded form, end-repaired, dA-tailed, and finally adapter-ligated for library construction and sequencing. Sequencing service was performed by Novogene Ltd. If transcription mistakes are present in the original RNA template, the error will be detected on every concatenated copy, periodically in the very same position; if errors are made by technical inaccuracies of the methods (by reverse transcription, PCR amplification, or sequencing), they will be scattered along the cDNA concatenated units in different positions; therefore can be easily eliminated by bioinformatic selection (
Fritsch et al. 2018
) (
see below
).
For CirSeq sample preparation we have used non-treated (NT, plants grown at 21 °C, 16 h/8 h light/dark) and 1-day 37 °C-treated seedlings. The HS time-point was chosen because (i) transcription is generally suppressed at early time points of HS (TMHT/1h) but later (at TMHT/1d) broadly resumed (
Szadeczky-Kardoss et al. 2022
), and (ii) RNA-seq indicated that erroneous transcripts accumulate to higher levels after 1 d HS (
Supplementary Fig. S1C
). Notably, the TMHT/1d regime impacts very mildly the HS-sensitivity phenotype of
tfIIs-1
or
upf
single and double mutant plants (
Szadeczky-Kardoss et al. 2022
), reducing the chance of pleiotropic indirect effects.
Bioinformatic analyses of circle-sequencing data
Raw circle-sequencing data of at least 3 biological replicates was analyzed according to previously described pipelines and codes (
Chung, Verheijen, Zhang, et al. 2023
),
https://github.com/
LynchLab/TranscriptErrors. Raw paired-end reads were trimmed with Cutadapt (
https://doi.org/10.14806/ej.17.1.200
). Tandem repeats were identified and consensus sequences of the repeats from the same read were created. The consensus sequences were mapped to the
A. thaliana
TAIR10 (v.56) cDNA dataset and the breakpoints (the ends of the initial RNA fragments before circularization) were identified. The consensus sequences were realigned to the RNAPII transcriptome with Tophat2 according to the breakpoints (
Kent 2002
). A refining step was implemented for the non-perfectly aligned sequences to search for a better breakpoint position before re-mapping these reads with Tophat2. Lastly, every mapped base was examined for identifying substitutions, insertions, and deletions, with the following conditions: (i) it needs to be part of at least 3 repeats on the same read; (ii) it is at least 3 nucleotides away from the ends of consensus; (iii) the sum of quality scores for the base is higher than 100; (iv) the identity of the repeats containing the base is at least 90%; (v) less than 1% of all base calls for the given position are different from the reference genome.
The Circo plot was created with Circos software (
Krzywinski et al. 2009
). Data were calculated for the metagene plots with deepTools (
Ramirez et al. 2016
). Sections of the metagenes were adjusted to the
A. thaliana
average transcript section lengths, namely the 5′UTR, the CDS, and the 3′UTR ratios (155:1391:242 nt,
Srivastava et al. 2018
;
Pucker et al. 2019
). The possible impact of errors on the amino acid changes was analyzed with SNPEFF software (
Cingolani et al. 2012
). We used the data from our previously published RNAseq dataset (
Szadeczky-Kardoss et al. 2022
) for the preliminary error rate analysis with the help of the webtool Alfred (
https://www.gear-genomics.com
) (
Rausch et al. 2019
). Gene ontology (GO) analysis was performed with the web tool g:Profiler (
https://biit.cs.ut.ee/gprofiler/gost
) (
Raudvere et al. 2019
) (
Supplementary Table S1
).
RNA extraction and RT-qPCR
RNA extraction and RT-qPCR were performed as previously described (
Szadeczky-Kardoss et al. 2022
): total RNA was purified by grinding about 30 mg of seedlings in 600 µL of extraction buffer (0.1
m
glycine–NaOH, pH 9.0, 100 m
m
NaCl, 10 m
m
EDTA, 2% SDS) and extracting it with equal volumes of phenol–chloroform (pH 4.3) and chloroform; subsequently, RNA was precipitated with ethanol and resuspended in sterile water. For RT-qPCR assays, 5 μg total RNA was treated with DNase I according to the manufacturer instructions (Ambion AM2222,
www.thermofisher.com
), then precipitated in ethanol and resuspended in sterile water. 1 μg of DNase I-treated RNA and random primer was used for the first-strand cDNA reaction (NEB, E6300S,
neb.com
). qPCRs were done using qPCR Master Mix (NEB, M3003S,
neb.com
). qPCR reactions were run in a LightCycler 96 (Roche) real-time PCR machine. At least 3 biological samples were assessed in each experiment.
P
-values were calculated using unpaired 2-tailed Student's
t
-test to assess the significance of differences;
t
-test comparison of samples is shown where considered relevant. For primers and statistical analysis, please see
Supplementary Table S4
.
RNA transcriptome and AS analysis
Total RNA samples obtained from Col-0,
tfIIs-1
,
upf1-5
,
upf3-1
,
tfIIs;upf1
, and
tfIIs;upf3
mutants under non-treated (NT), 1-hour (1 h) and 1-day (1 d) conditions from seedlings have been prepared for paired-end Illumina sequencing in 3 biological replicates each. Raw RNA-seq data have been made available in the SRA repository (repository link). We aligned reads to the Arabidopsis genome (TAIR10.v56) with HISAT2 (
Kim et al. 2015
). Differential expression analysis was made with StringTie (
Pertea et al. 2015
), Cuffquant, and Cuffdiff (
Trapnell et al. 2012
,
2013
). Heatmaps were made with Cluster3.0 (
de Hoon et al. 2004
) and Java Treeview (
https://bitbucket.org/TreeView3Dev/treeview3/src/master/
).
Alternative splicing analysis was performed with ASpli (v3.12) (
Estefania et al. 2021
).
For each gene, transcript exon coordinates were determined using Samtools (
Li et al. 2009
) and StringTie (
Pertea et al. 2015
), based on the RNA-seq alignment files. In silico transcript sequences were generated from the
A. thaliana
reference genome using these exon coordinates. Transcript identifiers, exon positions, sequences, and expression values (FPKM) were stored in a MySQL database and used for downstream steps. To predict amino acid sequences and support further examination,
A. thaliana
CDS and protein sequences were utilized. In silico translated proteins were generated from the predicted transcripts, enabling comparative studies and annotation refinement. For the further study of AS transcripts, ORFs, 3′UTR lengths, and introns within 3′UTRs, specific Python3 programs were used (
https://github.com/galnora/as_analysis
). GO term data of AS transcripts is made available in
Supplementary Table S3
.
Protein extraction and western blotting
For protein assays, heat-treated or non-treated 7-day seedlings were homogenized in protein extraction buffer (150 m
m
Tris–HCl, pH 7.5, 6
m
urea, 2% SDS, and 5% B-mercaptoethanol), treated for 5 min at 95 °C and cell debris removed by centrifugation at 18,000 ×
g
at 4 °C for 10 min. The supernatants were resolved on 12% SDS-PAGE, transferred to Hybond PVDF membranes (GE Healthcare) and subjected to western blot analysis. Antibodies used for detection were the following: anti-sHSP-CI antibody (AS07 254, Agrisera), anti-HSP90-1 antibody (AS08 346, Agrisera), and anti-HSP101 (AS07 253, Agrisera); as secondary antibody we used monoclonal HRP-conjugated anti-rabbit (A6154, Sigma-Aldrich). The proteins were visualized by chemiluminescence (ECL kit; GE Healthcare) and quantified by Image Lab 5.1 (Bio-Rad); protein signals have been normalized to Rubisco large subunit (RbcL). Statistical analysis is shown in
Supplementary Table S4
.
Insoluble aggregate purification
For protein aggregate purifications, first total protein extracts were prepared by homogenization of 0.1 g fresh plant material in 2.4 mL aggregate isolation buffer [25 m
m
HEPES, pH 7.5, 200 m
m
NaCl, 0.5 m
m
Na EDTA, 0.1% (v/v) Triton X-100, 5 m
m
ε-amino-
N
-caproic acid, 1 m
m
benzamidine], first using a mortar and pestle and then a Cole-Parmer PTFE glass tissue grinder. The soluble and insoluble fractions were separated by centrifugation at 16,000 ×
g
for 15 min at 4 °C. The soluble fraction was prepared by adding 2× SDS-PAGE sample buffer and heating for 5 min at 95 °C. The insoluble pelleted fraction was washed 5 times in the aggregate isolation buffer containing 0.1 g of quartz sand (Sigma-Aldrich); an additional wash was performed with aggregate isolation buffer without Triton X-100. The pellet containing the insoluble protein aggregates was resuspended in 400 mL 2× SDS-PAGE sample buffer, heat-treated for 5 min at 95 °C, and clarified by centrifugation at 1500 ×
g
for 1 min before gel loading. Samples were separated by SDS-PAGE and stained with Coomassie brilliant blue; the whole lanes have been quantified by Image Lab 5.1 (Bio-Rad) and ratios calculated. Statistical analysis is shown in
Supplementary Table S4
.
